newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE observes 'fair' vote, questions Moslem protest.
newsitem.headline: OSCE observes 'fair' vote, questions Moslem protest.

text.p: International supervisors of Bosnia's first post-war elections said on Sunday independent monitors found them largely free and fair, all but dismissing a Moslem refusal to accept results from Serb areas.

France and Germany joined Richard Holbrooke, U.S. architect of Bosnia's peace process who witnessed Saturday's polling, in praising the elections, piling pressure on the Moslems to drop their challenge over alleged Serb ballot fraud.
Bosnian Serbs responded to the Moslems' move by ordering local election committees to stop counting votes in Serb areas, for which tens of thousands of Moslem refugees cast ballots.
But the counting resumed a few hours later following intervention by the election overseers, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

International sponsors had braced for post-election protests and obstruction by Bosnian factions still polarised after 43 months of war, and said they were confident disputes would be ironed out in coming days.

The OSCE said all of Bosnia's factions knew in advance the elections would not be perfect and the preliminary evidence gave no cause to annul the results in any of Bosnia's divided Moslem, Croat and Serb-dominated sectors.

"They were almost entirely free of abuse. The international (OSCE-affiliated) observers, according to our preliminary reports, have been well satisfied with the arrangements they observed," said OSCE spokeswoman Agota Kuperman.

"All major political parties including the (Moslem) SDA agreed to participate in these elections, knowing full well that a state of perfection in so far as political behaviour is concerned had not been achieved."
Preliminary results from balloting for a three-person Bosnian presidency from Moslem, Serb and Croat communities as well as inter-ethnic parliaments are due on Monday.
An international monitors' report will influence a decision later this month on whether to certify the results. Steps to form power-sharing institutions and pass a 1997 budget would then begin.

The protest by Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic's Party of Democratic Action was addressed to the U.N. Security Council, ultimate arbiter of Bosnia's peace process, but Holbrooke and other international officials shrugged it off.

"We always knew there would be protests about the elections...But this was a general protest clearly (drafted) before the elections," Holbrooke told reporters in Sarajevo on Sunday. "It is not a big deal."
Izetbegovic issued a statement later citing "reports of serious irregularities" in Serb-area voting but strikingly made no mention of the SDA's vow not to recognise the results.

"We will submit relevant evidence to proper forums for the necessary response. We seek that all efforts be undertaken to correct any serious deficiencies or irregularities," the president's mild statement said.
SDA spokesman Ismet Grbo said the party objected to an apparent excess in the number of registered Serb voters over the number in Bosnia's 1991 census, the basis of the elections.

Jovan Zametica, adviser to acting Bosnian Serb president Biljana Plavsic, said the SDA's move was predictable because Moslems, as the demographically largest nation in Bosnia, "have always tried to dominate it".
Plavsic's ultra-nationalist Serb Democratic Party presided over the conquest of part of Bosnia from which Moslems and Croats were evicted in 43 months of war.

Although she has heartened peace coordinators by pledging Serb participation in an inter-ethnic government, analysts believe the pro-secession Serbs will try to paralyse the endeavour at every opportunity.
Holbrooke capitalised on momentum from the unexpectedly calm and orderly elections by arranging for Izetbegovic to meet Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in Paris in about three weeks' time.
Milosevic's role as patron of Bosnia's minority Serbs is regarded as crucial to get them to cooperate in stitching the country back together again.
